description: We want to build a nice UI for Fire & Ice Events.
summary:
Landfall turns NISAR radar data into guided, self-playing stories on a map. Radar sees through cloud, smoke and polar night, but a radar image is hard to read. Our app explains, chapter by chapter, what the radar found – and what it could not.

The main story follows the volcano Krasheninnikov on Kamchatka. It woke up in August 2025 after more than 400 quiet years, five days after a magnitude 8.8 earthquake, and it is still erupting. Ten NISAR passes from June to October 2026 show where new rough ground – fresh lava – keeps appearing. Comparing two passes reveals where lava is still moving, and two polarisations tell lava from vegetation. In the same months the camera satellite saw mostly cloud on 30 of 59 photo days.

Two more stories use the same frame: a megafire in France, mapped through the smoke (98 % confirmed by photos taken later), and an iceberg tracked through the Antarctic winter.

Every number is sourced or measured. Every physical assumption is listed in the app under "Show adjustments", and illustrations are labelled as such – so people who are not radar experts can trust what they see.
details:
What it does. The app opens on a full-screen 3D map and tells a real event as a story in chapters. If the reader does nothing, the story plays by itself: the camera flies, timelines run, and one highlighted sentence per chapter carries the story forward. A click hands over the controls: timelines to scrub, map views to switch (radar brightness, change since the last pass, new bright ground, two-polarisation colour), and an "Explore" tab with the calibrated data.

How NISAR is used (volcano Krasheninnikov).

- Backscatter (L2 GCOV, HH and HV, 10 m): ten passes from the same orbit, one every 12 days. Shown in decibels on one fixed scale, so dates can be compared.

- New bright ground: pixels at least 6 dB brighter than on the first pass that stay bright on every later pass – a screening of where fresh, rough lava appeared, in hectares per pass.

- Two polarisations: a colour picture from HH and HV separates blocky lava, vegetation and smooth bare slopes.

- Coherence (L2 GUNW, 12-day pairs): old lava keeps its radar "fingerprint", the active channel loses it every time. NISAR picks out the moving lava on its own, through cloud and at night.

- Limits, stated in the app: NISAR did not see the first blast (its pictures of this volcano start later), and it measures neither heat nor lava thickness.

What surrounds the radar. The earthquake and tsunami that came first, the eruption with an ash column drawn to scale, a hundred years of eruptions at neighbouring volcanoes, NASA FIRMS heat detections for every day (the first one six minutes before the reported start of the eruption), Sentinel-2 photos and infrared glow, and a "weather strip" that shows how often cameras were blinded by cloud.

Two more stories in the same frame. The Gironde megafire (France, July 2026): NISAR passed twice while it burned; coherence mapped 31,682 ha, 98 % confirmed by Sentinel-2. Iceberg A-81 (Antarctica): found and measured about every five days in the polar night; calibrated HH, HV and VV backscatter.

Honesty as a design rule. Every researched fact links to its source. Every chapter lists its physical assumptions and formulas under "Show adjustments" (for example decibel conversion, coherence, phase to distance d = −φλ/4π, tsunami speed √(g·depth)). Illustrations – moving lava, ash column, wave fronts – are labelled as not measured. Gaps are shown as gaps.

Benefits and intended impact. Teachers, journalists and emergency staff can follow a real event without knowing what "backscatter" means and still see real measurements. Scientists get an honest record of limits. The story frame is reusable: a new event needs a data folder and chapter texts, not new software.

How it is creative. Self-playing radar stories with a guided tour; 3D lava running along radar-flagged paths; a camera-weather strip next to radar passes; a clock to the minute from earthquake to eruption.

What we considered. Plain language; no scrolling walls of text (details open on demand); reduced-motion support; every number checked against its data file.

Tools. Python (NumPy, rasterio, h5py, pyproj, Pillow, httpx, earthaccess) for data preparation; TypeScript, React, Vite and MapLibre GL JS for the app; pytest and ruff for checks. An AI coding assistant (Claude) helped write code and texts.
